summary: Describes using the AES Galois Message Authentication Code (GMAC) in IPsec ESP and AH to provide data origin authentication without confidentiality. GMAC is based on the Galois/Counter Mode of operation, so it can reuse hardware built for that mode. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: IPsec can encrypt a packet, check that it came from the claimed sender, or do both. This RFC adds the missing case: checking the sender without encrypting the content. It uses GMAC, the authentication part of AES-GCM, so an implementation that already does AES-GCM can reuse most of its code and hardware. The RFC also says exactly how the nonce and the authentication tag are laid out in the packet.

subtitle: Using AES-GMAC in IPsec to authenticate packets without encrypting them.

tldr.problem: IPsec can encrypt a packet, authenticate it, or do both, but a deployment that wants authentication without confidentiality has no standard way to get it that reuses the hardware and code already built for AES-GCM.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two transforms built on GMAC, the message authentication part of AES-GCM: ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC for ESP and AUTH_AES_GMAC for AH. The ESP payload carries an 8-octet IV and a 16-octet tag, and the nonce is a 4-octet salt plus the IV.
tldr.outcome: IANA assigned transform identifiers 9, 10 and 11 for AH with the three AES key sizes and 21 for ESP. The RFC requires an automated key management system, because reusing a nonce with the same key destroys the security of GMAC.

facts.label: ICV size
facts.value: 16 octets, the AES-GMAC tag, never truncated

facts.label: Salt size
facts.value: 4 octets, constant for the life of the security association

facts.label: KEYMAT size
facts.value: Four octets longer than the AES key: 20, 28 or 36 octets

today: RFC 4543 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification for using AES-GMAC in IPsec ESP and AH.

sections.title: Authentication Without Encryption
sections.content:
This document describes the use of AES-GMAC mode as a mechanism for data origin authentication in ESP and AH. These methods are called ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC and AUTH_AES_GMAC respectively. ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC is a companion to the AES Galois/Counter Mode ESP, which provides authentication as well as confidentiality, and it is intended for cases in which confidentiality is not desired. Like GCM, GMAC is efficient and secure, and is amenable to high-speed implementations in hardware. The two transforms are designed so that the incremental cost of implementation, given an implementation is AES-GCM-ESP, is small.

The document does not cover implementation details of GCM or GMAC; those details can be found in the GCM specification, along with test vectors.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec can encrypt a packet, check that it came from the claimed sender, or do both. This RFC adds the missing case: checking the sender without encrypting the content. It uses GMAC, the authentication part of AES-GCM, so an implementation that already does AES-GCM can reuse most of its code and hardware.

sections.title: What GMAC Is
sections.content:
GMAC is a block cipher mode of operation providing data origin authentication. It is defined in terms of the GCM authenticated encryption operation. The GCM operation has four inputs: a secret key, an initialization vector, a plaintext, and an input for additional authenticated data (AAD). It has two outputs, a ciphertext whose length is identical to the plaintext and an authentication tag. GMAC is the special case of GCM in which the plaintext has a length of zero, so the zero-length ciphertext is ignored and the only output is the authentication tag.

The same nonce and key combination MUST NOT be used more than once, since reusing a nonce and key combination destroys the security guarantees of AES-GMAC. Because of this restriction it can be difficult to use this mode securely with statically configured keys. For the sake of good security, implementations MUST use an automated key management system, such as IKE in either version two or version one, to ensure that this requirement is met.
sections.plainLanguage: GMAC is the message authentication half of AES-GCM, with the encryption turned off: the plaintext has length zero and the only output is an authentication tag. The tag proves the data came from the holder of the key and was not changed. As with any stream-cipher-like mode, the same nonce must never be used twice with the same key.

sections.title: AES-GMAC in the ESP Payload
sections.content:
The AES-GMAC algorithm for ESP is defined as an ESP combined mode algorithm rather than an ESP integrity algorithm. It is called ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC to highlight the fact that it performs no encryption and provides no confidentiality.

The RFC gives the reason: ESP makes no provision for integrity transforms to place an initialization vector within the Payload field, only encryption transforms are expected to use IVs. Defining GMAC as an encryption transform avoids this issue and allows GMAC to benefit from the same pipelining as GCM. Like all ESP combined modes, it is registered in IKEv2 as an encryption transform, or Type 1 transform. It MUST NOT be used in conjunction with any other ESP encryption transform within a particular ESP encapsulation, and if confidentiality is desired then GCM ESP SHOULD be used instead.

With ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC, an explicit Initialization Vector is included in the ESP Payload at the outset of that field. The IV MUST be eight octets long, and for a given key it MUST NOT repeat. The most natural way to meet this requirement is to set the IV using a counter, but implementations are free to set it in any way that guarantees uniqueness, such as a linear feedback shift register. The sender can use any IV generation method that meets the uniqueness requirement without coordinating with the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: ESP has no place to put an initialization vector for an integrity-only transform, so the RFC defines GMAC as a combined mode, the same kind of slot that encryption uses. The name says what it does: no encryption, but authentication. The payload then starts with an 8-octet IV that must never repeat for a given key, followed by the payload itself and the tag.

sections.title: The Nonce and the Data It Covers
sections.content:
The nonce passed to the AES-GMAC authentication algorithm is laid out as a salt followed by the initialization vector. The salt field is a four-octet value that is assigned at the beginning of the security association and then remains constant for its life. The salt SHOULD be unpredictable, that is, chosen at random before it is selected, but it need not be secret. The initialization vector field is the one described for the ESP payload.

Data integrity and data origin authentication are provided for the SPI, the (Extended) Sequence Number, the authenticated payload, the padding, the pad length and the next header fields. This is done by including those fields in the AES-GMAC additional authenticated data field. Two formats of the AAD are defined: one for 32-bit sequence numbers, in which the AAD is the SPI, then the sequence number, then the payload, padding, pad length and next header; and one for 64-bit extended sequence numbers, where the sequence number field is replaced by the extended sequence number. The choice between 32-bit and 64-bit sequence numbers is determined by the security association management protocol used to create the security association; for IKEv2 it is negotiated via Transform Type 5, and the default for ESP in the absence of negotiation is to use 64-bit extended sequence numbers.

The integrity check value consists solely of the AES-GMAC authentication tag. The tag MUST NOT be truncated, so the length of the ICV is 16 octets. The IV adds 8 octets to the packet and the ICV adds 16 octets; these are the only sources of packet expansion, other than the 10 to 13 bytes taken up by the ESP SPI, sequence number, padding, pad length and next header fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The nonce is a 4-octet salt plus the IV from the packet. The integrity check covers the SPI, the sequence number, the payload and the trailer fields, so a receiver can tell that none of them was changed. The tag itself is 16 octets and is never shortened. Together the IV and the tag add 24 octets to each packet.

sections.title: AES-GMAC in the Authentication Header
sections.content:
In AUTH_AES_GMAC, the AH Authentication Data field consists of the IV and the authentication tag. Unlike the usual AH case, the Authentication Data field contains both an input to the authentication algorithm, the IV, and the output of the authentication algorithm, the tag. No padding is required in the Authentication Data field, because its length is a multiple of 64 bits.

The GMAC nonce input is formed as described for ESP, and the GMAC AAD input consists of the authenticated data as defined in Section 3.1 of RFC 4302. Those values are provided to the algorithm along with the secret key, and the resulting authentication tag is used to form the ICV.
sections.plainLanguage: In the Authentication Header form, the header's authentication data field holds the 8-octet IV followed by the 16-octet tag. Unlike a normal AH, the field carries both an input to the algorithm and its output. The data that gets checked is the usual AH authenticated data, the headers of the packet.

sections.title: How IKE Supplies the Key and the Salt
sections.content:
This section describes the conventions used to generate keying material and salt values for ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC and AUTH_AES_GMAC using IKE versions one and two. The document does not specify conventions for using AES-GMAC in IKE Phase 1 negotiations, because a separate specification would be needed and an Encryption Algorithm Identifier would have to be assigned; implementations SHOULD use an IKE Phase 1 cipher at least as strong as AES-GMAC, and the use of AES-CBC with the same AES key size is RECOMMENDED.

The way the key length is indicated differs between AH and ESP. For AH, each key length has its own separate integrity transform identifier and algorithm name, and the IKE Key Length attribute MUST NOT be used with these identifiers. For ESP, there is a single encryption transform identifier, and the IKE Key Length attribute MUST be used with each use of it, with a value of 128, 192 or 256.

IKE derives keying material of arbitrary size, called KEYMAT, using a pseudo-random function, and keying material is extracted from the output string without regard to boundaries. The size of the KEYMAT for these transforms MUST be four octets longer than the associated AES key: 20 octets for a 128-bit key, 28 octets for a 192-bit key and 36 octets for a 256-bit key. In each case the first part is the AES key and the remaining four octets are used as the salt value in the nonce.
sections.plainLanguage: IKE supplies the key and the salt together. The keying material is four octets longer than the AES key, so 20, 28 or 36 octets, and the last four octets become the salt. In AH each key size has its own transform number and the key length attribute is not used; in ESP there is one transform number and the key length attribute says which size is in play.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The authentication coverage differs between AES-GCM-ESP and this specification, and it is worth pointing out that both specifications are secure. In ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC the IV is not included in either the plaintext or the additional authenticated data. This does not adversely affect security, because the IV field only provides an input to the GMAC IV, which is not required to be authenticated. In AUTH_AES_GMAC the IV is included in the additional authenticated data; this also has no adverse effect, since GMAC is secure even against attacks in which the adversary can manipulate both the IV and the message.

GMAC is provably secure against adversaries that can adaptively choose plaintexts, ICVs and the AAD field, under standard cryptographic assumptions. In short, a break of GMAC within its intended parameters implies a break of the underlying block cipher.

The most important security consideration is that the IV never repeats for a given key. This is handled in part by disallowing the use of AES-GMAC with statically configured keys. When IKE establishes fresh keys between two peers, separate keys are established for the two traffic flows; if a different mechanism establishes only a single key, there is a high probability that the peers will select the same IV values for some packets, so ESP or AH implementations that permit the same key for packets with the same peer MUST ensure that the two peers assign different salt values to the security association.

As with any block cipher mode, the security of all data protected under a given security association decreases slightly with each message. To protect against this, implementations MUST generate a fresh key before processing 2^64 blocks of data with a given key. That limit is impossible to reach when using 32-bit sequence numbers. For each message, GMAC calls the block cipher only once.
sections.plainLanguage: The most important rule is that the IV must never repeat for a given key, which is why the RFC insists on an automated key management system. The second rule is that a key should not protect too much: a fresh key is needed before 2^64 blocks of data have been processed with it, and the two directions of a connection must use different salt values if they share a key.

sections.title: Design Rationale and the Registered Identifiers
sections.content:
This specification was designed to be as similar to AES-GCM-ESP as possible. The design and implementation experience from that specification is reused, and all three AES key sizes are included since AES-GCM-ESP supports all of them and the larger sizes give future users more high-security options.

IANA assigned the following IKEv2 parameters. For the use of AES-GMAC in AH, the integrity (type 3) transform identifiers 9, 10 and 11 were assigned for AUTH_AES_128_GMAC, AUTH_AES_192_GMAC and AUTH_AES_256_GMAC. For the use of AES-GMAC in ESP, the encryption (type 1) transform identifier 21 was assigned for ENCR_NULL_AUTH_AES_GMAC.
sections.plainLanguage: The design follows AES-GCM-ESP closely so that an existing implementation can reuse it, including support for all three AES key sizes. IANA registered three numbers for the AH form, one per key size, and one number for the ESP form.

fields.name: Initialization Vector
fields.desc: Eight octets, used as an input to the authentication algorithm and never repeated for a given key.

fields.name: Integrity Check Value
fields.desc: Sixteen octets, the AES-GMAC authentication tag. It is never truncated.

fields.name: Salt
fields.desc: Four octets, assigned at the start of the security association and constant for its life. Unpredictable but not secret.

fields.name: Initialization Vector
fields.desc: The eight-octet IV carried in the packet.

viz.caption: THE IKEv2 TRANSFORM IDENTIFIERS IANA ASSIGNED
THE RULES AN IMPLEMENTATION MUST FOLLOW

items.title: Never repeat the IV
items.text: The same nonce and key combination must not be used more than once, or the security of GMAC is destroyed.

items.title: Use key management
items.text: An automated key management system such as IKE must supply the keys, so static keys are not usable.

items.title: Different salts per direction
items.text: Peers sharing one key must assign different salt values, or they may pick the same IV.

items.title: Rekey before 2^64 blocks
items.text: A fresh key must be generated before that many blocks of data have been processed with a key.
